newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Dec 9.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Dec 9.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's edition of The Wall Street Journal:
- Homestake Mining reached an agreement to buy Santa Fe Pacific Gold for about $17.40 a share in stock, or $2.3 billion.
- Financial markets fought back from a morning drop as comments from Fed chief Greenspan referring to "irrational exuberance" were tempered by a benign jobless report.
- Mutual fund investors didn't bolt from the stock market after Friday's decline, but evidence is growing that fund holders are getting nervous.
- Big airlines would get a $600 million yearly windfall and discount firms would be harmed under a user-fee proposal by large carriers to replace the ticket tax.
- Nine oil companies signed a deal with three governments that could unlock the oil wealth of the Caspian Sea basin.
- The labor market is softening but perhaps not quickly enough to allay concerns about inflation.
- The Fed chairman voiced scepticism about the idea of moving part of the Social Security trust fund's investments into the stock market.
- Microsoft is launching a TV-style upgrade of its on-line service as it aims to become a major media player.
- TWA 's search for a new chief has one remaining serious candidate, Virgin Express CEO Jonathan Ornstein.
- Kansas City Southern emerged as a key player in U.S.-Mexico trade with its surprise $1.4 billion bid last week for Mexico's busiest rail line.
- Hayes Wheels is expected to say it agreed to acquire control of Europe's top wheel maker for $240 million in stock and cash, plus assumed debt.
- Britain's government named conditions on the alliance between British Airways and American Air, but rival U.S. carriers called them inadequate.
- The Teamsters elect a president this week.
- Madison Avenue is looking at limits on alcohol and tobacco ads, amid fears of a government crackdown.

- Long derided for a single-minded focus on stability and income, investors are scooping up high-yield, emerging market and nondollar bonds like never before in a desperate attempt to match the steep gains of the stock market.

- The sale last month of $70 million of Marvel's junk bonds by Fidelity Investments and Putnam Investments saved the mutual fund companies about $14 million in extra losses on securities issued by a holding company of Ronald Perelman's struggling comic book company, Marvel Entertainment Group.
